title: Language and gender
subtitle: chairperson, firefighter, spokesperson, Ms
summary: Use gender-neutral English with confidence - firefighter for fireman, staffed for manned, Ms for Miss or Mrs - and know the difference between male and masculine, laddish and macho.

lesson.heading: Gender-neutral language
lesson.text: In professional contexts and elsewhere, we often take care to use **gender-neutral** language in English. Attention has focused on replacing 'male' words that have a **generic** meaning - words with male connotations that actually refer to people in general - with neutral items. **Chairman** has become **chair** or **chairperson**, and **salesman** has become **sales assistant**. In some cases, such as job descriptions, sexually neutral language is a legal requirement.

examples.text: **Sales assistants** are often well trained and can be very persuasive.

lesson.note: The aim is to make the language less stereotyped with regard to gender, and perhaps to alter gender-biased attitudes.

lesson.heading: How far should it go?
lesson.text: There is continuing debate between extremists and moderates about how far such revisions should go: whether they should affect traditional idioms such as **the man in the street** (a typical person) and **Neanderthal Man**, or apply to parts of words where the male meaning of *man* is no longer dominant, such as **manhandle** (handle roughly, using force) and even **woman**.

examples.text: **The man in the street** has little time for such issues.
Rewritten neutrally: **The average person** has little time for such issues.

lesson.note: Some people felt changing chairman was unnecessary, or that language change cannot be imposed artificially.

lesson.heading: Older usage and current usage
rows: to man a machine or place of work

lesson.heading: Titles and marital status
lesson.text: The vocabulary of marital status has also been affected, notably by the introduction of **Ms** as a neutral alternative to **Miss** or **Mrs**. It does not focus on whether a woman is married, so it is useful when you do not know a woman's marital status, or when she does not want people to know it.

examples.text: Please address the letter to **Ms** Alison Reid.

left.label: male, female
left.text: Used for gender classification, as in biology.
examples: The **male** cat is less aggressive than his sister.

right.label: masculine, feminine
right.text: Having qualities traditionally felt to be typically male or female.
examples: She always dresses in a very **feminine** way.

lesson.heading: Informal words for men and women
rows: an informal way of addressing a group of men and women
Do any of **you guys** fancy going out for a pizza tonight?
used by women to refer to a female friend
I'm meeting up with a few **girlfriends** this evening.
describes things girls and young women often enjoy without men - clothes, make-up and so on
They're having a **girlie** evening at home.
informal word for a boy or young man
He's having a night out with some of the **lads** tonight.
unpleasant behaviour thought typical of young men in a group, especially drinking
I can't stand that kind of **laddish** behaviour!
describes a man who likes to appear strong and doesn't show his feelings
He refuses to cry - it would spoil his **macho** image!

lesson.heading: he, she and they
lesson.text: A grammatical problem in this area is using **he** or **his** for a person of either gender. In *A government minister may have to neglect his family*, the minister could be a woman. You can write **his or her**, make the sentence plural, or use **their** as a generic pronoun.

examples.text: A government minister may have to neglect **his or her** family.
**Government ministers** may have to neglect **their families**.
A government minister may have to neglect **their** family.
examples.note: increasingly common and acceptable, though some people consider it incorrect

lesson.note: Some writers use the pronoun s/he instead of he or she.

lesson.text: In job advertisements and other official writing, neutral wording is not just polite - it can be a legal requirement.

exercises.prompt: Three ___ helped put out a fire at a disused warehouse last night.
exercises.explanation: Firefighter is the gender-neutral replacement for fireman.

exercises.prompt: A ___ for the Department of Education provided us with a statement.
exercises.explanation: Spokesperson replaces spokesman in current usage.

exercises.prompt: ___ wanted for house in Priory Street.
exercises.explanation: Cleaner is the neutral term, and job adverts require neutral language.

exercises.prompt: The helpline is continuously ___ even during holiday periods.
exercises.explanation: To man a place of work has been replaced by to staff it.

exercises.prompt: All our ___ are fluent in at least three languages.
The fibres in this garment are ___.
exercises.explanation: Artificial is the neutral alternative to man-made.

exercises.prompt: ___ today spend more time in cars than on the beat.
exercises.explanation: Police officer replaces policeman and policewoman.

exercises.prompt: This was a great step for ___.
exercises.explanation: Mankind is replaced by the human race or human beings.

exercises.prompt: The ___ has little time for such issues.
exercises.hint: (neutral for the man in the street)
exercises.explanation: The average person or the person in the street replaces the man in the street.

exercises.prompt: Match each older term with its current, neutral equivalent.
She always dresses in a very ___ way.
exercises.explanation: Feminine describes qualities traditionally felt to be typically female; female is a biological classification.

exercises.prompt: The ___ cat is less aggressive than his sister.
exercises.explanation: Male is used for gender classification in biology.

exercises.prompt: Do you ___ fancy meeting up later?
exercises.explanation: You guys is an informal way of addressing a mixed group of men and women.

exercises.prompt: The bar was full of loud, ___ young men.
exercises.explanation: Laddish describes unpleasant behaviour thought typical of young men in a group.

exercises.prompt: Ross likes to see himself as a tough ___ man!
exercises.explanation: A macho man likes to appear strong and does not show his feelings.

exercises.prompt: Anna's going away for the weekend with a few ___.
exercises.explanation: Women use girlfriends to refer to their female friends.

exercises.statement: Ms was introduced as a title that does not show whether a woman is married.
exercises.explanation: Correct - it is useful when you do not know a woman's marital status, or when she prefers not to reveal it.

exercises.statement: In the phrase 'male words with a generic meaning', generic means that the word refers only to men.
exercises.explanation: Generic means the word refers to people in general, even though it has male connotations.

exercises.prompt: Which wording belongs to older usage and which to current, neutral usage?
Rewrite this sentence to avoid assuming the minister is a man.
exercises.answer: Government ministers may have to neglect their families
exercises.explanation: Making the sentence plural is one way to avoid the generic his; his or her and their are the others.
